The Emiliany storefront and its integrations

I built the storefront in English and Spanish. I connected Medusa for accounts and orders, Odoo for customer contacts, Mautic for email preferences, and Zammad for support.

Explore Emiliany ↗

Services connected to Next.js

The Next.js storefront connects to these services.

G

Google

Authenticates customers who choose Google sign-in.

M

Medusa

Manages customers, products, carts and orders.

O

Odoo

Keeps customer contacts available to the business.

m

Mautic

Manages marketing contacts and email preferences.

Z

Zammad

Turns contact messages into support tickets.

Follow a checkout, sign-in, profile update, or support request.

Browsing and checkout

The storefront shows the collection. Medusa handles products, carts, and orders.

  1. 01
    Next.js storefront

    Browse jewelry in English or Spanish.

  2. 02
    Medusa commerce

    Load products and prices, manage the cart, and submit checkout.

  3. 03
    Customer account

    Find order history and manage profile and addresses.

Where does the catalog come from?

Medusa supplies the live catalog. The preview uses sample items. Odoo receives customer contacts, with product sync disabled.

Sign in with Google or email

Customers can sign in with Google or with an email and password.

  1. 01
    Continue with Google

    Google authenticates the customer through Medusa’s Google provider.

  2. 02
    Complete the account

    New customers accept the terms and privacy policy before Medusa creates their account.

  3. 03
    Return to the shop

    The storefront keeps the session in a secure HttpOnly cookie.

What if the customer already has an account?

Customers must enter their existing account password to link a Google sign-in with the same email address. Staff use a separate sign-in. Customers choose whether to receive marketing email.

Keeping customer details in sync

Medusa stores customer profiles. Background jobs update the other business tools.

  1. 01
    Save in Medusa

    Medusa saves profile changes and queues updates for the other tools.

  2. 02
    Update Odoo + Mautic

    Odoo receives contact details. Mautic receives contact details and marketing preferences.

  3. 03
    Sync email preferences

    Customers choose whether to receive marketing emails. The shop picks up opt-outs from Mautic.

Does a slow business tool hold up signup?

Customers can finish signing up while background jobs update Odoo and Mautic. The jobs retry failed updates. Newsletter signups go to Mautic alone. A customer record by itself gives no permission to send marketing email.

From message to support ticket

The contact form sends customer questions to the support queue.

  1. 01
    Send a message

    The customer fills out the storefront contact form.

  2. 02
    Validate on the server

    The contact API validates the request and uses Redis to limit abuse and duplicate submissions.

  3. 03
    Create a Zammad ticket

    The team handles the request in its support queue. Zammad sends the acknowledgement.

How are retries and replies handled?

The form blocks duplicate messages for 24 hours and holds uncertain deliveries for a later check. To add a follow-up to the support queue, customers can submit the form with their ticket number. Email replies to the acknowledgement do not go straight into Zammad.

I run the services on Antalos, my Kubernetes platform. I keep deployment settings in Git for review and use Argo CD to apply them.

Infrastructure lab

I set up and operate the servers, storage, and segmented network for Antalos. I use the lab to deploy services and troubleshoot problems from the hardware through the virtual machines. Watch the application tour →

Servers, storage, and networking

The rack holds a firewall, switch, shared storage, and three Proxmox hosts. Two Lenovo servers run beside a reused HP Omen with a GPU.

I buy used hardware and repair it or reuse parts. I route the cables through a Cat6 patch panel and use an APC UPS and a PDU for power.

3
Proxmox hosts
112 GB
combined host RAM
10 GbE
SFP+ service links

Hardware and roles

The network

OPNsense runs on a Beikong H31F with an Intel N150, 8 GB RAM, three 2.5 GbE ports, and two SFP+ ports. A Juniper EX3300-24T provides 24 gigabit copper ports and four 10 GbE SFP+ ports.

Dedicated firewall · Managed switching

2 × ThinkSystem SE350

Each Lenovo node has a Xeon D-2143IT with 8 cores / 16 threads and 48 GB ECC RAM. I use Proxmox on these servers to run Talos nodes, Debian workloads, and HAProxy VMs.

96 GB ECC RAM across the pair

Repurposed HP Omen

This Proxmox host has an Intel Core i7-9700KF and 16 GB of RAM. I plan to pass an RTX 3060 with 12 GB of VRAM through to a Debian VM for LLM inference and run Talos control plane and worker VMs on the same host.

GPU passthrough · Dedicated inference VM

A dedicated TrueNAS server

The 2U, four-bay NAS uses a Ryzen 3 2200G, a gigabit management link, and a separate SFP+ link. I use an APC SUA1500 UPS with an AP9630 network card and a 12-outlet PDU.

Shared storage · Networked UPS management

Keeping network traffic separate

Management uses dedicated gigabit access links on VLAN 20. The Proxmox hosts carry internal and DMZ service traffic over 10 GbE trunks on VLANs 30 and 40.

Traffic path into the rack

  1. UPLINKAT&T gatewayInternet connection
  2. ROUTE + FILTEROPNsenseVLAN routing and firewall
  3. DISTRIBUTEJuniper EX3300Access ports and tagged trunks
1 GbE / VLAN 20

Proxmox, Lenovo XCC, TrueNAS, and UPS management interfaces.

Service plane

Proxmox VM networks use SFP+ trunks. TrueNAS also connects over SFP+ for storage traffic.

Simplified network plan. Firewall rules control access between segments.

Proxmox → Talos → Antalos

My VM plan calls for a Talos control plane node and worker on each Proxmox host. The Lenovo servers also run HAProxy and Debian workloads for testing, Jellyfin, and Immich machine learning. An Intel Arc A310 goes to the media VM.

Proxmox runs the VMs, Talos runs Kubernetes, and Antalos defines the services on top.
